Photograph: Spanish Police/Reuters Opinion Spain Ceuta showed just how easy it is to divide Europe Paul Taylor The migrant influx prompted recriminations and a tit-for-tat dispute between Italy and Spain. Putin, Erdoğan and others will have taken note Wed 12 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 03.13 EDT Share W ithin hours of the first pictures of tens of thousands of migrants swimming the short distance from Morocco to the Spanish north African enclave of Ceuta hitting social media on 30 July, 22 European Union leaders , the Trump administration and Israel had piled on to criticise Madrid. The outbreak of hysteria and recrimination was a case study in 21st-century politics, driven by real-time images in a media echo chamber where populists set the agenda on migration, propagating fear, prejudice and demagogic proposals. Above all, the kneejerk reactions undermined trust between European allies and dealt a setback to EU efforts to jointly manage migration, counter people-smuggling and resist the weaponisation of migrants by non-EU countries. That Donald Trump and JD Vance should seize the opportunity to accuse socialist Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez of inviting the mass influx by allowing more than 1 million irregular migrants already working in Spain to apply for legal status is hardly surprising, given the US administration’s own relentless drive to detain and expel illegal immigrants. On the other hand, European leaders who signed a letter to the European Commision, criticising Spain and demanding an emergency meeting of interior ministers, should ask themselves how their behaviour helps the EU implement a coherent response to migratory pressures. Many are open to charges of hypocrisy, since Germany and Italy have, between them, regularised hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrant workers at the request of employers who need their labour as the home workforce dwindles. There was also a monstrous foreign policy double standard in the initial EU response. When Poland and Lithuania faced a sudden influx of irregular migrants from Belarus in 2021, the EU rallied behind its eastern members and imposed sanctions on Minsk’s authoritarian regime, which stood accused of weaponising displaced people from the Middle East. The previous year, the EU sent its Frontex border agency to help Greece repel a surge of migrants from Turkey at the countries’ shared border in Thrace, which had apparently been encouraged by Ankara to put pressure on the EU. View image in fullscreen Crowds gather near Fnideq on the Morocco-Spain border, 31 July 2026. Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty Images Yet this time, EU governments quickly fell into a divisive blame game, terrified by images that recalled the loss of control over borders in south-eastern Europe in 2015, when more than 1 million mostly Syrian refugees entered the bloc. Amid the internal finger-pointing, neither the EU leaders nor the European Commission dared question the role of Morocco , whose border guards apparently stood aside as more than 72,000 Moroccans, mostly young men, risked their lives swimming to Ceuta after seeing viral social media claims that “Spain is open”. The incident occurred on Morocco’s annual Throne Day when King Mohammed VI, who does not recognise Spanish sovereignty over the territories of Ceuta and Melilla, just happened to be visiting the nearby northern city of Tétouan, once part of the Spanish protectorate. Some commentators have called the stampede to Ceuta a “ Blue March ”, in reference to the mass Green March that the king’s father, Hassan II, launched in 1975 in an attempt to claim the vast territory of Western Sahara, then a Spanish colony. “In Morocco, nothing happens by chance,” says Anna Terrón Cusí, a senior fellow at the Migration Policy Institute and a former Spanish secretary of state for immigration. Even if the stampede to Ceuta started spontaneously with social media posts, she believes “this was a multi-actor, multi-factor event. It was more a geopolitical than a migration crisis.” Intra-European party politics played a big role. It was not surprising that the Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, should lead the assault on Sánchez. She heads up the hard-right Brothers of Italy movement and faces a domestic challenge in elections next year from a new, even further-right party, led by a retired general . Some Spanish and UK anti-immigration politicians rushed to Ceuta to take selfies, one from Reform UK doing a standup interview on the beach to cash in on the purported alien “invasion”. It was more bizarre that Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen, who heads a centre-left government, should co-initiate with Meloni the letter to Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, and say that the EU should consider suspending Spain from the Schengen area of open-border travel. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Preview latest after newsletter promotion A facade of European solidarity was restored after EU interior ministers held a hastily arranged videoconference. By that time, almost all the migrants had left Ceuta and returned to Morocco after realising that they had no chance of reaching Europe. The “ invasion ” had deflated. In fact, irregular migrant arrivals in Spain fell sharply last year, while across the EU they’re down for the second successive year, and far below the 2015 crisis peak. But the damage was done. Italy and Spain are now engaging in tit-for-tat passport and nationality controls on each other’s travellers, and Russian president Vladimir Putin, Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and King Mohammed himself will have noted how easily Europe panics and turns on its own members at the first sight of migrants on its beaches. Whether out of misinformation or malice, some EU ministers distorted the nature of the Spanish amnesty for undocumented migrants, labelling it a “pull factor” for mass migration. Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, claimed they were being granted Spanish and therefore European citizenship, rather than simply being given a chance to apply for temporary work visas. Europe faces what in game theory is called the “ prisoners’ dilemma ”, and in social sciences a “ collective action problem ” . EU countries have a shared interest in preserving the Schengen zone of free movement, with open internal borders vital to the smooth operation of the economy, well-managed external borders to deter irregular migrants and combat people smugglers, and legal migration routes to permit an inflow of workers needed by businesses as the European population ages and shrinks. Yet they keep undermining cooperation due to a seemingly irresistible short-term political interest in anti-migration grandstanding. Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? https://www.dw.com/en/indonesia-china-na.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IxUm China carries out frequent military drills around Taiwan [FILE: December 2025] Image: Taiwan Coast Guard/AFP Advertisement On August 12, an Indonesian frigate briefly joined a naval exercise with China's People's Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) in waters off Taiwan's east coast, with Taipei asking Jakarta for a reason why it joined the drill. Indonesian Navy frigate KRI I Gusti Ngurah Rai joined the PLAN guided-missile frigate Honghe for what Jakarta described as a "passing exercise." The maneuvers took place during Taiwan's annual Han Kuang military drill. An Indonesian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson said they were fully aware that the exercise's location "made it particularly sensitive," but stressed that its vessel's presence "was simply part of its transit route back to Indonesia." According to the Taipei Times , the Indonesian vessel was returning from Vladivostok, Russia after an exercise with the Russian navy. Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council condemned Beijing's "provocation" after China announced the drill on August 11. Taipei also requested "further details from the Indonesian government" from its Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Beijing considers Taiwan to be Chinese territory and has vowed to "reunite" the self-ruled island with the mainland, by using force if necessary . The People's Liberation Army has ratcheted up pressure on Taiwan with frequent military exercises around the island, especially since former US House Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei in 2022. Amid reactions from Taipei and Washington, the Indonesian Navy stated that its activities with the Chinese Navy were "not warfighting activities in nature" and "not intended as combat training." China's gray zone warfare in the Pacific To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Ying-Yu Lin, an associate professor at Taiwan's Tamkang University Graduate Institute of International Affairs and Strategic Studies, told DW that the Chinese exercise with Indonesia had little tactical significance. "It wasn't as practical as a joint maritime drill, but China wanted to claim its capability in the waters," he said. Indonesia dragged into sensitive geopolitics However, Ratih Kabinawa, a visiting research fellow at the Japan Institute of International Affairs focusing on Taiwan-Indonesia ties, told DW that regardless of the significance of the drills, Indonesia should have expected some reaction from Taiwan . "Like it or not, Indonesia is now dragged into this kind of geopolitical gambit," she said. Kabinawa added that passing exercises were among the lowest-level naval activities yet used by China to justify its intimidation of Taiwan. "Indonesia must also exercise caution in this regard," she said, adding that Jakarta should "not to be too naive," to assume that its participation in a "regular exercise" with China would not cause concern in Taiwan. Jakarta's nonaligned foreign policy in focus Indonesia has stood by its "free and active" foreign policy for over half a century, distinguishing itself from neighboring countries that align with China or the US. However, both Beijing and Washington want the world's largest island nation to be part of their Asia-Pacific strategy . Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto met with Elbridge Colby, a US undersecretary of defense, in Jakarta on the same day as the controversial passing exercise with China. While Prabowo also visits Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing, Jakarta has shown its willingness to accept US requests for blanket overflights, which allows US military aircraft access to Indonesian airspace. Chong Ja Ian, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, told DW that Indonesia's neutral stance is a product of pressure from superpowers. "The principle of free and active foreign policy wouldn't change much, but we'll wait and see how Jakarta operates it," he said. How China's rise is shaping Trump's strategy in Asia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Researcher Kabinawa said the current Indonesian administration lacks clear guidelines for interpreting its foreign policy amid intensifying geopolitical tension, especially across the Taiwan Strait. However, she added that it would be unlikely for Indonesia to be involved in any Chinese invasion scenario of Taiwan. "I would always remind everyone that there are 350,000 Indonesian citizens in Taiwan who need to be protected or maybe evacuated if that hypothetical scenario happens," she said. According to Taiwan's official data, Indonesians are the largest group of foreign residents in the country. "So I don't think Indonesia would get involved in being a combatant, but rather involved in trying to evacuate their citizens,” Kabinawa said. "That would risk the political and economic stability of the country [Indonesia] itself.” Iryanda Mardanuz in Jakarta contributed to this article. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Mark Carney arrives at the European parliament in Strasbourg, France, on 17 September 2026. Photograph: Justin Tang/The Canadian Press/AP View image in fullscreen Mark Carney arrives at the European parliament in Strasbourg, France, on 17 September 2026. Photograph: Justin Tang/The Canadian Press/AP Opinion Canada The Guardian view on EU-Canada relations: strategic ambition with lessons for Britain Editorial Mark Carney’s response to the challenges posed by an unreliable US president contains a clarity of vision that is lacking in post-Brexit Britain Thu 17 Sep 2026 13.48 EDT Last modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 14.15 EDT Share T here is no “associate membership” of the European Union , nor any blueprint for what such a thing might involve. It is a political hypothesis, describing a relationship of intimate strategic alignment with the EU, stopping short of actual membership, in ways that are significant but undefined. This week, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, invited Canada to be the first country to enjoy this putative status. In her state of the union speech, she spoke of a future relationship elevated “to the highest level possible”, reflecting an affinity of interests and values. Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, reciprocated the sentiment in a speech on Wednesday. Addressing the European parliament, he said the two sides should secure “strategic autonomy through deep cooperation” across a broad spectrum of interests: trade, defence, industrial capacity, science, space and AI. He proposed Canadian participation in the EU’s Erasmus student exchange programme and Horizon research scheme. There is a vast gap between the declaration of those ambitions and their formalisation in any kind of treaty. Negotiating even a relatively straightforward trade agreement with the EU can be heavy going, given the need to accommodate the rival priorities of 27 member states. Creating a more multifaceted partnership is arduous work, bedevilled by technical detail, as Britain has found when trying to settle the terms of its post-Brexit relationship with mainland Europe . View image in fullscreen Ursula von der Leyen. Photograph: Ronald Wittek/EPA That process has been complicated and slowed down by a deficit of trust. The Labour government has repudiated the venomous anti-Brussels ideology that drove the decision to leave the EU, but the Brexit deal inherited from the Conservatives was designed to work as an automatic ratchet, pulling the two sides apart. Reversing that mechanism takes a greater input of political energy and imagination than Sir Keir Starmer could muster. Andy Burnham has yet to rise to the challenge. The UK prime minister could learn from his Canadian counterpart. Both find their global positions weakened by Donald Trump’s contempt for traditional US allies. Their circumstances are not exactly alike. Canada and the US share the longest land border on Earth. Mr Trump denigrates his northern neighbour’s sovereignty, suggesting it become the 51st US state . He has provoked a pointless, costly trade war . The UK has not been spared tariffs and other diplomatic indignities, but it has not suffered quite the same degree of sustained rhetorical and economic aggression. Mr Carney has responded with a clear-eyed plan for geopolitical reorientation. He talks about a “ rupture ” in the international order and the challenge facing “middle powers” in a destabilised world shaped by rivalry between the US and China. He urges maximal cooperation between democracies that still value a system of multilateral alliances underpinned by international law and an understanding that reciprocal obligations can yield mutual benefits. That is the animating idea behind the new acceleration in Canada-EU relations. It is alien to Mr Trump, and he doesn’t like it. He has warned of yet more tariffs should the Ottawa-Brussels axis evolve into anything he deems economically unfavourable to the US. For the time being, this is all happening in the realm of rhetoric. But Ms von der Leyen’s speech and Mr Carney’s response are important as expressions of serious geopolitical ambition. The time is overdue for a British prime minister to show the same clarity of purpose. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? https://www.bursa.ro/nicusor-dan-sees-pr.text: On the first day of September, at Cotroceni, President Nicuşor Dan urged new magistrates to have the "courage of their own convictions." The head of state also stated that, regarding prosecutors, society's primary expectation concerns the fight against corruption-both "high-level and petty corruption." Speaking on appointments to leadership positions within prosecutors' offices, he noted: "I am waiting for the six-month mark since the appointment of the chief prosecutors to pass. The impression so far is that activity has gained momentum." The President also pointed to what he considers to be progress already achieved: "A positive development is that we have separated criminal investigations from television." He explained that the fact that key case documents no longer reach the public sphere via "leaks" represents, in his view, "a step forward." He did not present a tally of corruption cases at the time; he characterized his assessment of the new chiefs' work as merely an "impression," noting that he would wait for the six-month period to elapse. Two days later, during a meeting of the Superior Council of Magistracy, he stated that the "vast majority" of magistrates are honest individuals, but that suspicions of criminal activity within the system must be investigated. He added that the justice system requires balance, not "investigation for the sake of investigation." However, while the President holds a positive view of the chief prosecutors and the majority of magistrates, the reality on the ground contradicts him. In December 2025, the Recorder documentary "Captured Justice" brought to public attention allegations regarding the reshuffling of judicial panels, pressure exerted on judges, and major trials allowed to lapse due to the statute of limitations. Protests, testimonies from other magistrates, and meetings at Cotroceni Palace ensued. Nine months later, the mechanisms alleged at the time have not met with public responses commensurate with their gravity. Recorder demonstrated, among other things, how the leadership of the Bucharest Court of Appeal justified panel changes in corruption cases, while magistrates who spoke openly about the court's operations remained exposed. A recent case illustrates why discussing the justice system solely in terms of perception and public trust is insufficient. On September 22, after DIICOT detained Călin Georgescu for 24 hours in a new fraud case, Judge Vlad Andriescu of the Bucharest Tribunal rejected the request for pre-trial detention and ordered judicial supervision for 60 days. This is the same magistrate who, in the abuse-of-office case involving AUR First Vice-President Dan Dungaciu, issued a preliminary chamber ruling in September 2024, yet the written reasoning was not released until December 2025-a gap of approximately one year and three months. G4Media reported, citing judicial sources, that the statute of limitations for criminal liability had expired during this interval. The Bucharest Tribunal stated that the expiration of the statute of limitations must be determined by the court hearing the case. However, the delay in issuing the written reasoning remains a documented fact with a direct impact on the proceedings. Last week, an investigation by journalists from the Media Investigation Center highlighted another case. At the Craiova Court of Appeal, Judge Sorina Marinaş intended to refer a case to the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU); the case had originated from a complainant's challenge against a decision to close the investigation. Before a decision on the referral could be made, Prosecutor General Cristina Chiriac-of whom Mayor Nicuşor Dan, who appointed her, holds a favorable initial opinion, particularly given her status as a distant relative of Mirabela Grădinaru-requested a change of venue for the case. The High Court granted the request on September 15, and the case was transferred to the Bucharest Court of Appeal. Consequently, the questions prepared by Judge Sorina Marinaş were never submitted to the CJEU by her panel. The timeline reported by the Media Investigation Center is difficult to ignore. On September 14, the chief prosecutor of the Prosecutor's Office attached to the Craiova Court of Appeal recused himself from considering a potential request for a change of venue or recusal, as the prosecutor who had ordered the case closure was his wife. The deputy prosecutor subsequently appointed noted that she deemed neither recusal nor a change of venue necessary. Nevertheless, Prosecutor General Cristina Chiriac filed the request for a change of venue. The hearing date originally set by the High Court for September 17 was moved to September 15-prior to the scheduled hearing in Craiova where the CJEU referral was to be discussed. Curiously, according to the cited investigation, a document from the Prosecutor General's Office states that the complainant herself had requested the change of venue. The petitioner denied this. In the statement included in the attached document, Judge Marinaş notes that no such request existed in her panel's case file and that the petitioner had, in fact, expressed opposition to the change of venue. Under these circumstances, the Prosecutor General's Office should have explained the source of that notation and the document supporting it, but failed to do so. Instead of verifying a potential infringement of independence regarding the prosecutors' actions in filing the request for a change of venue, the Section for Prosecutors of the Superior Council of Magistracy (CSM) decided on September 18 not to refer the matter to the Judicial Inspectorate. The vote was four to three, according to the CSM's public document. The decision does not establish that Prosecutor General Cristina Chiriac's actions were lawful in every respect, but it indicates that no referral for an official review was made. Precisely for this reason, answers remain necessary regarding the request's handling, the urgency of rescheduling the hearing, and the disputed information found in official records. At the same time, the CSM denied entry to a journalist from CIM at the first hearing of the disciplinary proceedings concerning Judge Laurenţiu Beşu-who appeared in the December 2025 Recorder documentary. The hearing was postponed at the request of the Judicial Inspectorate. The dispute over the public nature of that hearing is separate from the Craiova case, yet it speaks volumes about the climate following the "Captured Justice" report: those who speak out and those attempting to monitor institutional reactions encounter, in turn, barriers that require public explanation. President Nicuşor is right to call upon young magistrates to show courage. Yet individual courage alone cannot fix a system where a written ruling is delayed by over a year, a potential referral to the CJEU is derailed by a change of venue, and the CSM refuses to review a contested action. If the Romanian justice system wishes to regain public trust, the response cannot simply be rhetoric about balance; instead, a verifiable explanation is required for every decision that alters the course of a case. Articol despre Superior Council of Magistracy (CSM), Justice System, Prosecutor General’s Office, Nicusor Dan, magistrates.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Marine Le Pen blows a kiss to supporters in La Fleche, in the Sarthe department, a day after announcing her candidacy for the 2027 French presidential election Photograph: Benoît Tessier/Reuters View image in fullscreen Marine Le Pen blows a kiss to supporters in La Fleche, in the Sarthe department, a day after announcing her candidacy for the 2027 French presidential election Photograph: Benoît Tessier/Reuters Opinion The far right Europe’s big election season is about to kick off. It could change everything Nathalie Tocci If far right nationalists gain power in four big countries simultaneously, we are in for a dramatic Trumpian tilt Tue 13 Oct 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 00.01 EDT Share W hen it comes to Europe’s economy or its peace and security, it is obvious that decision-making has to be done largely at the European level to be meaningful. Yet electoral politics is still conducted mostly at the national level. The silver lining of this mismatch is that from country to country in Europe we have governments with different political priorities and leanings. Unlike in the US, where one presidential election can radically change the entire country’s course, as we have seen so vividly under Donald Trump’s leadership, the same drama has not so far unfolded in Europe. This may be about to change. Pedro Sánchez rolled the dice in Spain last week, calling a snap election for next month after an unholy alliance of the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox and Catalan pro-independence party Junts blocked his big housing reform package in parliament. If the socialist prime minister, hailed by progressives globally but demonised by Europe’s right and Trump’s US, loses his election gamble, Spain could fall into the hands of a conservative/far-right coalition, which is currently ahead in the polls. In addition to Spain, France , Italy, Poland, Finland, Greece, Estonia and Slovakia will all head to the polls in the coming year. The four largest of these, France, Italy, Poland and Spain, could see far-right or nationalist populist parties either confirmed in power (Italy), returned to it (Poland) or elected for the first time (France and Spain). This could dramatically change the face of Europe. Europe has been tilting to the right for some time, with far-right parties entering coalition in different countries at different times. Centre-right and far-right groups are now able to form a majority in the European parliament, coalescing in particular around an anti-climate and anti-migration agenda. But while this tilt has slowed European integration, its policy effects have not been as rapid and radical as those we have seen in the US under Trump. This is because the rightward shift has so far not been homogeneous. In the Netherlands last year, Geert Wilders’s far-right Freedom party was punished at the polls and the liberals made a comeback. This year, Hungary’s slide into authoritarianism was halted, and is now being reversed, after Viktor Orbán was ousted in a landslide election. Most recently, in Sweden, support for the far right, which had backed the outgoing centre-right government, slipped. The opposition bloc, led by the Social Democrats, scraped a victory . So, while the rise of the far right is a continent-wide trend – Alternative für Deutschland’s recent victory in eastern Germany sent shock waves across Europe – it does not hold everywhere, at all times. But if the coming round of elections were to bring Marine Le Pen to the French presidency, confirm Giorgia Meloni as Italian prime minister, possibly backed by a coalition even further to the right than the current one, return the Law and Justice party to power in Poland, and produce a conservative/far-right government in Spain including Vox, the face of Europe could change dramatically. If all these countries, plus several smaller ones, elected far-right or nationalist populist governments, they would not reach a qualified majority able to steer the EU’s policy course. But they would form a blocking minority, putting an end to any ambition of deeper EU integration in such areas as finance, energy, defence and technology. View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham with Friedrich Merz in Berlin after Burnham ‘opened the door to Britain rejoining the EU’ Photograph: Filip Singer/EPA And it is not just a question of numbers. These far-right leaders would have a galvanising and radicalising effect on each other, propped up by Maga America and Silicon Valley’s algorithms. The common perception outside Italy is that Meloni has mellowed in power. To the extent that this is true, it is in no small measure because she has been surrounded by the likes of Emmanuel Macron, Donald Tusk and Sánchez, among others. If these leaders were replaced by the likes of Le Pen, Jarosław Kaczyński and Alberto Núñez Feijóo, backed by Vox’s Santiago Abascal, Meloni herself would act differently, more in line with her true political instincts. All this could trigger not simply a slow erosion of the European integration project – a muddling through with the unambitious agenda we have seen in recent years – but a hollowing out, if not an outright implosion. The EU as we know it would struggle to retain its purpose, especially if no agreement is reached on its next seven-year budget in the coming months. The irony is that European political heterogeneity persists, but outside the EU it is not only Canada that wants more proximity. More importantly, the UK may have begun the slow journey of retracing its steps. It took 10 years for a British prime minister to call a spade a spade, publicly recognise that Brexit has done more harm than good and open the door to rejoining the EU, as Andy Burnham has now done. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion It has taken a decade to remember the purpose of European unity and the emptiness of petty nationalism – just as Europe risks losing the memory of its dark past and teeters on the brink of falling apart. Now is perhaps the moment for the UK to remind its European neighbours what it means to be out there, all alone. Nathalie Tocci is a Guardian Europe columnist Explore more on these topics The far right Opinion Europe Spain Italy France Marine Le Pen Giorgia Meloni comment Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Reuters/EPA View image in fullscreen Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Reuters/EPA Opinion Brexit Brexiters can’t cope with the fact that Putin was cheering them on Rafael Behr Russian meddling probably didn’t affect the referendum result – but the Kremlin’s motives for wanting to undermine the EU still matter Tue 13 Oct 2026 11.21 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 13.43 EDT Share R ussian territorial aggression against Ukraine didn’t feature much in the Brexit referendum campaign. It made headlines briefly when Boris Johnson blamed Moscow’s 2014 annexation of Crimea on the European Union . According to the Vote Leave frontman, Vladimir Putin’s land grab was a consequence of Brussels making foreign policy “on the hoof” and having “pretensions to running a defence policy”. The logic of that position was that Kyiv had no right to choose its own allies and that European democracies should never have supported Ukrainian aspirations to escape submission to Moscow. It is the appeasement fallacy: if only the west acquiesced to Putin’s conviction that Kyiv is a Russian city and that Ukraine is not a proper country, he would not want to suffocate his neighbour’s independence. That notion is refuted by all the evidence of campaigns to coerce countries deemed by the Kremlin to be errant possessions since the collapse of the Soviet Union. When Nigel Farage repeated the EU-provocation theory of the Ukraine war during the 2024 general election campaign, one prominent defender of Ukrainian sovereignty described the Reform UK leader’s assertions as “ahistorical drivel” and “Kremlin propaganda” . That stalwart friend of Kyiv was one Boris Johnson. There is nothing unusual about Johnson contradicting himself. His talent as a political communicator came from the ability to hold whichever view was expedient to him in the moment and, for the duration of that moment, appear to hold it sincerely. In a more generous reading, he rose to the occasion of Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, understanding events in their proper geopolitical perspective (and with access to classified intelligence reports), which afforded a different reading of Putin’s motives. In 2016, his focus had been wilfully myopic. The goal of maximising Eurosceptic votes meant reaching for any argument that presented Brussels in a negative light. If that involved narrating the cause of a conflict on the other side of the continent in warped terms that matched the Kremlin story, so be it. Putin despised the EU for his reasons; the leave campaign despised it for theirs. Johnson was not minded to interrogate whether that alignment of enmities discredited his cause. This is the context in which Andy Burnham’s recent assertion that Russia meddled in the referendum needs to be understood. The prime minister said it was inconceivable, given all the evidence of Kremlin interference in elections around the world, that the toolkit of subversion would not have been deployed in support of Brexit. That is not a controversial claim to anyone with a glancing awareness of Russian foreign policy and the means by which it is pursued – the swarms of bot accounts flooding social media with falsehoods; dirty money channelled to extremists; industrial dissemination of conspiracy theories and stoking of intercommunal tensions to undermine social coherence, deplete trust in democracy and make it less functional. No candidate who was knowingly complicit in that process will admit as much. But even those who were unaware that their cause was boosted by Kremlin troll farms have incentives to deny it. No one wants their heroic victory recast as useful idiocy in service of a hostile power. Conservatives have called Burnham’s intervention “dangerous and divisive”, which could be interpreted as a denial that interference happened or just as a preference that it not be mentioned to protect delicate pro-Brexit sensibilities. Farage’s feelings were certainly hurt. He called the prime minister a liar and described the whole thing as a “Russia hoax” – the formula Donald Trump applied to well-substantiated allegations that his 2016 presidential campaign got a helping hand from Moscow . The Reform leader can’t be too surprised by the idea of Kremlin influence in British politics. His party’s former leader in Wales is serving a jail term for taking bribes from Russian spies. The backlash forced Downing Street to clarify that the prime minister didn’t mean to cast aspersions on the legitimacy of the referendum result. That is the right position when there is no way of knowing what impact, if any, foreign meddling might have had. The views that interference happened and also that the leave campaign would have prevailed anyway are compatible . Some remainers might seek comfort in the idea that Britain’s democracy was hijacked and diverted through clouds of Russian-induced false consciousness to the wrong destination. The banal truth is that the Eurosceptic side won enough arguments and voters made their choice freely. Brexiters didn’t need any outside help to turn latent anti-immigration sentiment into active hostility to free movement across European borders. The Russia dimension is more relevant when it comes to a geopolitical argument that the pro-European side failed to land. In June 2016 it was hard to make the peril of strategic isolation for Britain, self-exiled from the club of European democracies, no longer confident in the transatlantic relationship, seem vivid or imminent. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more after newsletter promotion Trump’s first presidential election was five months away. The full extent of his scorn for the US’s allies and his admiration for authoritarians would not be clear for years. His propensity to behave like a private client of the Putin regime can still shock, even if it no longer surprises, as with the sanctions-busting deal he struck last week to import billions of dollars of Russian diesel. The hope, entirely vain, is to depress pump prices and assuage voter frustration ahead of midterm elections in November. On top of the cash infusion for the Kremlin’s war effort, Trump added a bonus of rhetorical venom for Volodymyr Zelenskyy, calling for regime change in Kyiv. He blames Ukrainian targeting of Russian refining capacity for rising global energy costs because his narcissistic ego resists the truth – that his war in Iran has been a disaster for the US and a boon for its enemies. The fact that Russia is an Iranian ally , providing Tehran with intelligence support to resist US military pressure, is no impediment to Trump’s commercial collaborations with the Kremlin. The exact character and motive involved in that relationship may never be elucidated. But there is no need to seek out hidden levers of influence that may not even exist when publicly available data paints a full enough picture. Trump and Putin are two greedy despots who recognise no boundary between national interest and self-enrichment. They see law not as a restraint on government but as an instrument to be wielded by powerful leaders against perceived enemies. Their approach to domestic politics is gangsterish, based on networks of patronage and tribute. Their view of foreign affairs is imperial, based on the belief that strong states have natural title to territory in their immediate vicinity, and that big countries can trade in the fate of smaller ones like casino chips. It is as obvious to Trump that Moscow has a seigneurial right over Ukraine as it is that he should be allowed to decide who governs Venezuela and who sells its oil. That ethos leads inevitably to competition for resources where rival spheres of influence meet and, if there is no international framework for resolving that competition, to war. This is the lesson, learned the hard way in the 20th century, that became the foundational idea of the European project – the principle of swapping nationalistic rivalry for mutually beneficial cooperation within a common framework of law. That is why Putin and Trump cannot understand the EU and why they hate it. And that is why the error of Brexit is more pronounced today than it was when the question was put in a plebiscite, and why Burnham is right to draw attention to the fact that Russia had a preferred side. The prime minister is also right when he says that rejecting the possibility of restoring closer ties with the EU would be “a dereliction of duty”. Many falsehoods were propagated in the referendum campaign, but none greater than the leavers’ boasts of patriotism, when their agenda was certain to make Britain poorer and weaker. A decade into the error, there is no patriotism in pretending that Brexit has worked or in crying betrayal when anyone suggests a reversal. Isolation from the rest of Europe is the result that Britain’s enemies wanted in 2016. Sticking to that path is the route they would choose for Britain again today if they had a vote.
